Lytham St Annes.region: Lytham St Annes and the Fylde coast
Lytham St Annes.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Fylde coast
s1loc: Lytham St Annes anchors the genteel end of the Fylde coast, where the Victorian St Annes Pier, opened in 1885, looks out over a long flat beach and the listed green Lytham Windmill stands beside the Lytham Green seafront. Grade I listed Lytham Hall, a Georgian country house set in 78 acres of parkland, and the salt-water Fairhaven Lake draw visitors across the year on this stretch of Lancashire coast.

The leisure layer runs from boating and watersports on Fairhaven Lake through the wide sands and the formal Ashton Gardens to the Lowther Gardens pavilion at Lytham. Royal Lytham and St Annes Golf Club, founded in 1886, is a championship links that has hosted The Open eleven times and is set to host again in 2028, drawing golf crowds and tour parties to the resort each season.

Heritage and culture run through the conservation streets of Lytham and St Annes, with the windmill museum, the Lowther Pavilion theatre and a busy events calendar. Lytham Festival fills Lytham Green with major summer concerts, while St Annes hosts the Kite Festival on the seafront, the proms and motor-themed weekends that bring day visitors out along the promenade.

Underpinning the trade is a settled base of seafront hotels, guest houses and Bed and Breakfast businesses across Lytham and St Annes, with golf tour operators, coach firms and guides working the Fylde. Rail links from St Annes-on-the-Sea and Ansdell and Fairhaven feed the line via Blackpool, while neighbouring Blackpool, Poulton-le-Fylde and Preston widen the day-trip catchment around the resort.

Worksop.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Dukeries
s1loc: Worksop bills itself as the Gateway to the Dukeries, the cluster of ducal estates in north Nottinghamshire on the edge of Sherwood Forest. The National Trust's Clumber Park spreads over 3,800 acres of parkland, heath and woods with its Gothic chapel and serpentine lake, while nearby Sherwood Forest and the ancient Major Oak draw the Robin Hood crowd to the country a few miles south of the town.

The leisure layer runs across the Dukeries country, from cycling and walking trails through Clumber Park to the lake and pleasure grounds, with family days out at Welbeck and the wider Bassetlaw countryside. The Chesterfield Canal threads through Worksop on the River Ryton, giving towpath walks, boat trips and waterside leisure that keep operators busy through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture sit thick on the ground here, from the 12th-century Worksop Priory and its Priory Gatehouse on Potter Street to the eccentric, untouched Edwardian interiors of Mr Straw's House, a National Trust property on Blyth Grove. The Harley Gallery and the Portland Collection at Welbeck show fine art and treasures gathered by the Dukes of Portland over centuries.

The visitor trade rests on country-house estates, hotels and guest houses across Worksop and the Dukeries, with Thoresby Hall and the surrounding parkland pulling day-trippers and coach parties. Worksop railway station links the town along the line toward Sheffield and Lincoln, and nearby Retford, Mansfield and Chesterfield broaden the catchment for visitors touring north Nottinghamshire and Sherwood Forest.

Leigh.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Wigan borough
s1loc: Leigh sits in the Metropolitan Borough of Wigan, where Pennington Flash Country Park spreads its 70-hectare lake across former colliery land and records over 230 bird species. The Flash is one of eight sites forming The Flashes of Wigan and Leigh, the first National Nature Reserve in Greater Manchester, designated by Natural England in 2022, and a major draw for walkers, anglers and birdwatchers near the town.

The leisure layer centres on Leigh Sports Village, a 12,000-capacity stadium and complex that hosts Leigh Leopards rugby league and the Manchester United Women's side, alongside its athletics track, swimming pool and sports centre. Pennington Flash adds a golf course, sailing and play areas, while Lilford Park and the towpaths of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal give green space and waterside walks across the town.

Heritage and culture run through Leigh Spinners Mill, an intact double cotton mill described as the finest of its late era, with a restored steam engine, a heritage centre, a 110-seat cinema and a computer museum. Leigh Library on Civic Square houses the Turnpike Gallery and Derby Room, showing work by local and international artists alongside the town's heritage displays.

The visitor trade is shaped by home games and fixtures at Leigh Sports Village, drawing rugby and football crowds who fill local hotels, pubs and guest houses around the town. Bus links run through Leigh toward Manchester and Wigan, with the wider Wigan borough on the doorstep, and neighbouring Wigan, Hindley and Atherton widen the day-trip and event catchment around the town.

Bexhill-on-Sea.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Sussex coast
s1loc: Bexhill-on-Sea is best known for the De La Warr Pavilion, a Grade I listed Modernist building of 1935 designed by Erich Mendelsohn and Serge Chermayeff, often called Britain's first major Modernist public building. Free to enter on the seafront, its galleries, auditorium and roof terrace front a two-mile promenade of beach huts and deck chairs that defines this corner of the East Sussex coast.

The leisure layer runs along the seafront and through Egerton Park, with its boating lake, tennis, bowls and play areas beside the shore. The Sovereign Light Cafe on the front, the shingle and sand beaches, and the gentle Edwardian gardens give families and day visitors plenty to do, while the wider 1066 Country around the town adds coast and countryside for activity-led trips through the season.

Heritage and culture run deep here, from a charter granted by King Offa of Mercia in 771 to Bexhill Museum on Egerton Road, with its early motor-race cars, costume and natural history. Bexhill is the birthplace of British motor racing, where the 8th Earl De La Warr staged the first races along De La Warr Parade in 1902, an event still marked by the town's motoring festival weekends.

The visitor trade rests on seafront hotels, guest houses and Bed and Breakfast businesses, with the De La Warr Pavilion drawing arts, music and comedy crowds across the year. Bexhill railway station links the coastal line between Hastings and Eastbourne, and neighbouring Hastings, Eastbourne and Hailsham broaden the catchment for visitors touring the 1066 Country coast of East Sussex.

Altrincham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Trafford
s1loc: Altrincham, an old Cheshire market town in the borough of Trafford, is anchored by the National Trust's Dunham Massey, an 18th-century house set in a 300-acre deer park with a working 17th-century mill and waterwheel. Home of the Earls of Stamford until 1976, the estate runs as a year-round draw with garden tours and a winter light trail that pulls visitors out to the edge of the town.

The leisure layer centres on the celebrated Altrincham Market, a covered market trading since 1920 and reinvented in 2014 as a food and design destination drawing the region's best traders. The Stamford Quarter blends retail with the Everyman Cinema, while Stamford Park, John Leigh Park and the trails around Dunham Massey give green space and family days out across the season.

Heritage and culture run through ten conservation areas including The Downs, Bowdon and the Old Market Place, with the Altrincham Garrick Playhouse, established in 1914, staging drama, comedy and musicals. The long-running Altrincham Festival each summer brings a parade and a two-day music and family event through the town, adding to a busy local events calendar.

The visitor trade rests on town-centre hotels, guest houses and a strong food and hospitality scene, with the Metrolink tram from Altrincham running into central Manchester in around half an hour. The rail and tram interchange and the wider Trafford catchment feed visitor flows, while neighbouring Stretford, Urmston and Wilmslow widen the day-trip draw around the town.

Urmston.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Trafford
s1loc: Urmston, with neighbouring Flixton and Davyhulme, sits in the borough of Trafford a short way south of the Trafford Centre. The town has a revived centre around Eden Square and a clutch of listed buildings recorded on the National Heritage List, set close to the Manchester Ship Canal and the green corridors that thread through this part of Greater Manchester.

The leisure layer runs across Abbotsfield Park, with its miniature railway, and the Davyhulme Park and Flixton golf courses, while Davyhulme Millennium Nature Reserve gives wetland and woodland walks along the western bank of the Manchester Ship Canal. The monthly Urmston Artisan Market at the Golden Hill car park brings street food, vintage and crafts to the town across the year.

Heritage and culture sit in the conservation streets and the listed buildings of Urmston, Flixton and Davyhulme, with the nearby Trafford Centre adding a major leisure anchor. Its 20-screen Odeon cinema, the first Selfridges store outside London, indoor crazy golf, a Laser Quest arena, bowling and Europe's largest food court draw visitors from across the region into the borough on the town's doorstep.

The visitor trade leans on the leisure pull of the Trafford Centre and the green and waterside spaces around Urmston, with bars, taphouses and the converted Steamhouse station building anchoring the town centre. Rail links run from Urmston station toward Manchester, and neighbouring Stretford, Altrincham and Salford widen the day-trip and event catchment across Trafford and Greater Manchester.

Grantham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Lincolnshire
s1loc: Grantham sits in south Lincolnshire close to the National Trust's Belton House, a 17th-century Grade I listed country house set in 1,300 acres of gardens and parkland where deer roam. A short drive away, Woolsthorpe Manor is the birthplace and family home of Sir Isaac Newton, the 17th-century farmhouse where he formed his theories of gravity and light, both anchoring the town's visitor draw.

The leisure layer runs from the gardens, adventure playground and trails at Belton House to Wyndham Park on the banks of the River Witham just north of the town centre. Across the county border the medieval Belvoir Castle looms over the Vale of Belvoir with its grounds and events, while the surrounding countryside gives walking, cycling and family days out across the season.

Heritage and culture centre on Grantham Museum, which tells the story of the town and its famous figures Sir Isaac Newton and Margaret Thatcher, alongside the soaring St Wulfram's Church and the historic Angel and Royal coaching inn on the High Street. The market and its events calendar keep the town centre busy through the year for visitors and day-trippers.

The visitor trade rests on hotels, country-house stays and golf resorts such as Belton Woods, with the National Trust estates pulling steady coach and day-trip traffic. Grantham railway station sits on the East Coast Main Line with fast links to London and the north, and neighbouring Newark, Stamford and Melton Mowbray broaden the catchment for visitors touring south Lincolnshire and the Vale of Belvoir.
